name: Cassia fistula (fruit emulsion or syrup, by mouth)
short: Pregnant rats (not people): smaller offspring. Emulsion in children: no clinically significant side effects in two small trials (81 and 109). Syrup trials give no adverse-event data.
text: Human safety data are limited to two small randomised trials in Iran of Cassia fistula emulsion in children with functional constipation. In 81 children aged 4 to 13 given the emulsion or mineral oil for 3 weeks, safety was assessed by clinical adverse effects, and neither treatment caused clinically significant side effects; anal leakage of oily material was an important complication with mineral oil, and children given the emulsion did not complain of it. In an open-label trial in 109 children aged 2 to 15 given the emulsion or polyethylene glycol for 4 weeks, which evaluated the safety of both, neither caused clinically significant side effects. The abstracts of the two trials of Cassia fistula syrup against lactulose, in 70 older adults and in 66 people with chronic kidney disease, give no adverse-event data; in the kidney-disease trial, blood urea nitrogen and creatinine fell within the syrup group. In a different product, a decoction of Cassia fistula pod with nutmeg arils and jaggery given to 31 women with period pain, no side effects were reported. In a study in pregnant rats (not people), an aqueous extract given by mouth throughout pregnancy caused no abortions or newborn anomalies, but offspring height and weight were reduced at two doses, and in the mothers' blood after delivery the liver enzyme ALT rose at the highest dose; in tissue from the newborn rats, significant liver inflammation was found at the two highest doses and also in the group given only the solvent. The authors call the extract safe in pregnancy but say the solvent confounded the tissue findings and more research is needed. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
